pattern: (is not available for Minecraft|servers are having trouble|Something went wrong during the server installation|Java install-script failed|Java installation failed|wget or curl is required|variables\.txt not present|Incorrect modloader specified|did not agree to Mojang's EULA)
note: The install script gave up before the server started, so no mod was ever loaded. Kept specific so a genuine mod-load crash does not match.

pattern: (Unable to access jarfile|Could not find or load main class|Invalid or corrupt jarfile|^Error: could not open|The Minecraft server \.JAR is missing|Missing game jar at)
note: The JVM never started -- it could not open or identify the jar it was told to run. 'Error: could not open' is the launcher's message for an unreadable @argfile and is anchored to line start on purpose: the launcher emits it as the whole line, while every mod line carries a timestamp prefix, and an over-broad match here turns a textbook clientside crash into INCONCLUSIVE.

pattern: (Could not find parent layer for module|Failed to find run file at|Failed to find startup arguments using run script path)
note: The modloader itself failed to bootstrap: the JVM started but the server never did. Forge's SecureModuleClassLoader looks a read module's configuration up among its direct parents only, so the ServerStarterJar's synthesised boot layer cannot find java.base and throws before FML exists.

pattern: (java\.lang\.OutOfMemoryError|insufficient memory for the Java Runtime Environment|Cannot allocate memory|Killed\s+"?\$?JAVA)
note: The run died for lack of memory rather than because of the mod. A mod can be memory-hungry, but running out of memory is not evidence that it needs a client.

The decisive signal, and the one thing the expensive boot exists to catch: the server loaded the mod and then died reaching for a client-only class. Outranks every excuse below -- a clientside mod may phone home AND die on a client class, and this must still win. Known gap: Fabric intermediary names (class_NNNN) are not matched, because that scheme is intermediary for every class and not only client ones, so a pattern would trade these false negatives for false positives.

pattern: (Missing or unsupported mandatory dependencies|Unmet dependency listing|Incompatible mods found|requires .{1,80} or above|requires any version of|requires version .{1,80} of |ClassMetadataNotFoundException|ClassNotFoundException: org\.spongepowered\.asm\.launch\.MixinTweaker)
note: A mod refused for unsatisfied required dependencies never got a fair test: it was rejected before its own code ran. The largest single failure class measured -- 36 of 112 kept logs in 2026-07-30, and Quilt's 'requires version [x, y) of z' phrasing alone was 63 of 200 published crash logs in 2026-08-29.

The sandbox refusing a mod the network. Boots run --network none and that isolation is the entire guarantee, so a mod whose loader reaches the internet at startup is certain to die here and nowhere else, making the crash a property of the harness. 15 of 200 published crash logs (2026-08-29).

pattern: (InvalidInjectionException|InvalidMixinException|MixinApplyError|MixinTransformerError|FAILED during APPLY|Critical injection failure|Mixin transformation of .{1,120} failed)
note: A mixin that could not be applied or injected: the jar and the Minecraft it was booted on disagree about what exists, so the mod's own server code never ran. Stays below client-only-class -- a mod reaching a client-only class THROUGH a mixin is a genuine signal.

pattern: (Unhandled solver error|\(0 valid options, 0 invalid options\)|Quilt Loader: Failed to load)
note: The modloader's dependency solver giving up, so nothing was loaded to judge. Quilt's phrasing shares nothing with Fabric's, which is why dependency-failure does not reach it.

The staged jar and the runtime disagree about the loader itself. log4j-core is the most valuable member and belongs here for the opposite reason: its absence is not the mod's doing at all, so a console reaching for it means the runtime we assembled is broken. All 90 boots against one poisoned NeoForge 21.11.45 / MC 1.21.11 cache entry died this way, a library and a server-side building mod among them.

The platform marks the server unsupported while the jar's own descriptor declares server/both. The two disagree, so neither is evidence -- this is the caution the old hardcoded fold carried as a report note, and it must outrank both confirming rules below.
The mirror image: the platform marks the server required while the jar declares client-only. Same reasoning, opposite direction.

The jar's own descriptor says client-only -- Fabric's environment=client, or a Forge/NeoForge dependency demanding side=CLIENT of the platform. The mod's own author said it, which is why this confirms without a boot.
Modrinth declares server_side: unsupported. CurseForge has no such field and always reads 'unknown', so this only ever fires for Modrinth projects.
